content:
Dear Halden Pay Hiring Team,

I am applying for the Senior Data Engineer – Data Platform role. Across nine years in data engineering, I have built and operated production platforms for e-commerce, logistics and payments, with a focus on dependable pipelines, clear data contracts and trusted warehouses. Halden Pay’s focus on a shared platform and reusable frameworks is a strong match for the work I have done.

At Lukovac Freight Hub, I own the platform ingestion layer across around 140 Airflow DAGs and have helped improve reliability and speed across the warehouse. I migrated more than 400 transformations to dbt, adding tests, documentation and incremental models; the nightly build fell from 5 hours 10 minutes to 1 hour 35 minutes. I also introduced data contracts that reduced broken-pipeline incidents from about nine per month to two, and built a Kafka streaming pipeline processing around 30 million events daily. These projects have involved operating production systems, improving data quality and taking responsibility for problems through the on-call rotation.

My earlier work at Kovalent Pay is especially relevant to Halden Pay’s business. I built PySpark reconciliation jobs on AWS EMR to process around 1.2 TB of daily files, reducing month-end manual reconciliation from about three days to four hours, and designed a Redshift warehouse with more than 30 fact and dimension tables for finance and risk. I have also contributed fixes and tests to an open-source Airflow provider. My experience is with AWS and Snowflake rather than Google Cloud, but it includes comparable cloud data platforms alongside the Python, SQL, Airflow, dbt and modelling work at the heart of this role.

Halden Pay’s values of ownership, collaboration and reducing unnecessary complexity resonate with how I approach platform work: making systems easier to operate, sharing context with colleagues and building foundations that teams can rely on. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience could contribute to the Data Platform team.

Kind regards,
Lena Varga-Holm

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is clear, professional, well structured, and appropriately tailored to Halden Pay’s Data Platform role. It uses strong quantified evidence: 140 Airflow DAGs, 420+ dbt models, reduced runtime, reduced incidents, 30 million daily events, and 1.2 TB of daily processing. The progression from platform engineering at Lukovac to payments-focused work at Kovalent Pay is especially persuasive. The final paragraph aligns well with Halden Pay’s ownership, collaboration, and pace-oriented culture. The main content limitation is that advanced Python and SQL, large-scale query or workload optimisation, governance, and reusable-platform engineering are not stated as directly as they could be.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is highly parseable: it uses standard headings-free prose, conventional paragraphs, plain text, and no tables, columns, graphics, or unusual formatting. It includes important keywords such as Data Platform, production systems, Python, SQL, Airflow, dbt, Kafka, PySpark, AWS, Snowflake, data quality, data contracts, data warehouse, modelling, and open-source. AI screening probability is high for the core platform, orchestration, cloud warehouse, streaming, payments, and open-source requirements. Screening may be weaker for the exact concepts “advanced Python,” “query optimisation,” “dimensional modelling,” “reusable frameworks,” and “governance,” because some are demonstrated through examples but not named explicitly. The candid acknowledgement of AWS/Snowflake rather than Google Cloud is accurate and preferable to overstating GCP experience.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: Alignment is strong. The letter demonstrates production data-platform ownership, large-scale cloud data warehousing, Airflow and dbt, streaming, data quality, data contracts, payments data, dimensional modelling, AWS, Snowflake, and open-source contribution. It also connects the candidate’s experience to Halden Pay’s shared-platform mission and values. Google Cloud is not present, but the candidate has relevant comparable-cloud experience through AWS EMR, S3, Glue, and Snowflake. The candidate material does not establish graph modelling or Portuguese, so these are genuine gaps rather than document defects. Query optimisation on large datasets is also not clearly evidenced in the supplied candidate material; the letter should not claim it specifically unless the candidate can substantiate it. The letter could make the connection to reusable frameworks and platform features for analysts, data scientists, and BI colleagues more explicit without inventing experience.
critique.improvement_instructions:
MINOR / HIGH-VALUE ENHANCEMENTS:
1. In the second paragraph, after the sentence ending “responsibility for problems through the on-call rotation,” add a sentence that explicitly connects the experience to the role’s reusable-platform focus, for example: “This work strengthened shared platform capabilities rather than creating one-off pipelines, giving downstream teams more reliable, reusable foundations.” Use this only as a summary of the documented platform work; do not claim collaboration with data scientists or BI colleagues unless separately supported.

2. In the third paragraph, make the dimensional-modelling keyword explicit. Change “designed a Redshift warehouse with more than 30 fact and dimension tables for finance and risk” to “designed a Redshift cloud data warehouse using dimensional modelling and a star schema, with more than 30 fact and dimension tables for finance and risk.”

3. In the third paragraph, make the comparable-cloud evidence more ATS-readable. Change “My experience is with AWS and Snowflake rather than Google Cloud, but it includes comparable cloud data platforms” to “Although my production experience is with AWS and Snowflake rather than Google Cloud, it includes comparable cloud data platforms: AWS EMR, S3 and Glue for large-scale processing, and Snowflake as a managed cloud data warehouse.” This remains fully supported by the CV and avoids implying GCP experience.

4. In the second or third paragraph, add one concise sentence naming the candidate’s Python and SQL scope, using only supported evidence: “My work combines Python and SQL across large-scale batch processing, warehouse transformation, CDC, and production pipeline optimisation.” This improves keyword coverage without claiming unsupported query-level optimisation. Do not add the exact claim “query optimisation on large datasets” unless the candidate can provide a truthful example of query tuning.

5. In the final paragraph, align the culture wording more closely with Halden Pay’s stated values. Change “Halden Pay’s values of ownership, collaboration and reducing unnecessary complexity” to “Halden Pay’s values of Together, Ownership and Pace—sharing context, taking responsibility, and reducing unnecessary complexity.” Keep the following explanation because it credibly supports those values.

Lena Varga-Holm

critique.content_quality_feedback: This is a strong, credible cover letter with a clear senior-level narrative and several quantified achievements. It demonstrates production ownership, platform-scale engineering, data quality, cloud warehousing, batch and streaming systems, and relevant payments experience. The examples are more persuasive than generic claims, particularly the dbt migration, incident reduction, streaming volume, reconciliation improvement, and warehouse design. The main content weakness is repetition: the Google Cloud/AWS comparison is stated twice in consecutive sentences, which makes the third paragraph feel less polished. The letter also gives limited direct evidence of query optimisation, collaboration with analytics or BI stakeholders, governance or access policies, and evaluating open-source tools, although some related experience is present in the candidate material.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is ATS- and parser-friendly: it uses standard headings and plain text, includes the target job title, and contains relevant keywords such as production data platforms, Python, SQL, Airflow, dbt, Kafka, data contracts, data quality, cloud data platforms, AWS EMR, S3, Glue, Snowflake, dimensional modelling, and open-source Airflow contributions. Its AI-screening probability is good because the evidence is specific and quantified rather than keyword-stuffed. ATS alignment would improve if the exact requirement terms were used where supported, especially “cloud data warehouse,” “production data platform,” “data modelling,” “data quality standards,” “reusable frameworks,” and “open-source practices.” The duplicated Google Cloud comparison should be removed because it reduces clarity without adding keywords.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The letter aligns well with the core role. It shows experience designing and operating a production data platform at scale, cloud warehouse design, Airflow and dbt, Python and SQL, dimensional modelling, batch and streaming pipelines, data contracts, data quality, and relevant fintech/payments work. It also supports the company values: the discussion of platform reliability, on-call ownership, shared foundations, and reducing complexity maps well to Ownership, Together, and Pace. The candidate's Airflow provider contribution supports curiosity about open-source practices. Comparable cloud experience is shown through AWS EMR, S3, Glue, Snowflake, Docker, and production platform work, although Google Cloud itself is not shown. The letter does not establish graph modelling or Portuguese; these are gaps in the candidate material, not defects that can be fixed by rewriting. Query optimisation on large datasets is only indirectly evidenced through runtime, warehouse, and database-load improvements and should be made more explicit only to the extent supported by the existing material.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL:
1. In the third paragraph, delete the repeated sentence beginning “My experience is with AWS and Snowflake rather than Google Cloud...” because the preceding sentence already makes the same point. Replace the two-sentence ending with one concise, evidence-based sentence such as: “Although my production experience is with AWS and Snowflake rather than Google Cloud, I have operated comparable managed cloud data platforms, including AWS EMR, S3, Glue and Snowflake, alongside the Python, SQL, Airflow, dbt and data-modelling practices central to this role.”

2. In the second paragraph, make the existing production-operations evidence more explicit by changing “These projects have involved operating production systems, improving data quality and taking responsibility for problems through the on-call rotation” to “These projects involved day-to-day operation of a production data platform, enforcing data quality through tests and contracts, and ownership through a one-week-in-six data-platform on-call rotation.” This uses evidence from the candidate information and more directly matches the job’s “own” and “day-to-day running” language.

3. In the second paragraph, replace the broad sentence “My work combines Python and SQL across large-scale batch processing, warehouse transformation, CDC, and production pipeline optimisation” with a more concrete sentence using the documented scale and outcomes: “I use Python and SQL across large-scale batch processing, warehouse transformation and CDC, including a 1.2 TB/day reconciliation workload, a 420-plus-model dbt warehouse, and CDC changes that reduced replica CPU during loads from approximately 70% to 25%.” This improves ATS and human-reader alignment without claiming unsupported query-optimisation expertise.

MINOR:
4. In the final values paragraph, connect the candidate’s existing examples more directly to Halden Pay’s stated values by changing “making systems easier to operate, sharing context with colleagues and building foundations that teams can rely on” to “making systems easier to operate, sharing context through data-platform office hours, mentoring engineers, and building reusable foundations that downstream teams can rely on.” These examples are supported by the candidate information and better reinforce Together, Ownership and Pace.

5. In the third paragraph, change “I have also contributed fixes and tests to an open-source Airflow provider” to “I contributed two merged pull requests to an open-source Airflow provider, fixing a pagination bug and adding tests.” This gives the open-source evidence greater specificity and uses the strongest documented wording.
